This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundational work by Brylinski and Karshon, we investigate the concept of prequantization within the framework of differential stacks and associated Lie algebroids. Furthermore, various applications of this construction have been discovered, particularly in relation to quantization problems. In addition to prequantization, another structure known as polarisation has been introduced within the context of differential stacks and Lie algebroids and its properties examined. Notably, problems arising from the geometric quantization of compact complex manifolds lead to a specific type of polarised stack, and the corresponding Lie algebroid problem has been reformulated in this setting.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows and those that aren't.  Mass growth rates for these cores are found to be indistinguishable, but a significant difference emerges when examining cores with outflows (CO bright sources).  These sources exhibit higher masses and compactness, likely due to denser local conditions.  Crucially, sources with outflows demonstrate measurable mass growth rates, in contrast to those without outflows which show mass contraction or stability.  This distinction may be explained by higher opacities in more dense sources, shielding them from radiative feedback and allowing for inward motion.  Core density profiles are found to be largely convergent, but with a notable exception: sources with outflows exhibit significantly higher opacities, leading to different mass evolution patterns.  This hypothesis is supported by radiative transfer modeling, which accurately reproduces observed far-infrared spectra when incorporating differences in core opacities.  This study provides evidence that sites of massive star formation are found more frequently than previously believed, in contrast to the traditional view that such formations are exceptions to the rule.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system that remains unchanged over time, such as time-series data and spatial fields. Our research introduces a novel approach to studying time-invariant random fields, utilizing the spectral properties of the spherical Bessel functions, which serve as the Fourier transform of indicator functions of balls, using the Bochner theorem. This method allows us to analyze the properties of the distribution of masses of uniform measures defined on the surface of a ball in relation to weak support properties. Specifically, we determine the minimal spherical shell indicators on the sphere, resulting in constructs that are equivalent in law to the uniform distribution, and we establish their properties regarding independence and recurrence relations, which replace the common multi-step recurrences in their one-step variant. These results have implications for efficient simulation, maximum likelihood estimation, and likelihood-free inference methods, including those based on indirect inference.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements, theoretical analysis, and computer simulations, we investigated the impact of base plate roughness on the stress relaxation of liquid foams after the removal of a stress. The release of stress occurs when a constrained foam is suddenly released from between two plates, and we measured the resulting interface displacement. We used the Dissipative Particle Dynamics method to create stress relaxation simulations for our research. The measured interface displacement was found to be directly related to the logarithm of time following the sudden release of stress. The rough surfaces caused the stress to dissipate more quickly than on smooth surfaces, and this dissipation was influenced by the roughness size and the size of the bubbles, but not by the bubble volume fraction or plate separation. The stress on the smooth interface was hydrodynamic in nature, while the rough surfaces created additional friction that resulted in increased stress dissipation. This interaction led to a decrease in interface displacement and could be seen in the stress relaxation simulations as well.

This report details our methods that earned third place in the detection category of the 2019 ISIC Challenge. Our approach utilized a pre-trained deep learning model, specifically an EfficientNet, to extract high-level features from input images. These features were then fed into a support vector machine classifier, enhanced with outlier detection techniques using the local outlier factor algorithm and sample importance estimation via the hit rate. Notably, our ensemble method of combining multiple efficientnet models ranked second overall in the challenge, securing second place in the detection metric and third place in the accuracy metric.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in this study. When the lighter outer fluid exerts higher pressure than the denser inner fluid, the interface becomes unstable and forms the "elastic fingers" that penetrate the inner cell. A theoretical model is developed to investigate this problem by treating a growing finger as a narrow channel, and results from this model are shown to match direct simulation data under specific conditions. Membrane properties significantly influence finger patterns, and in some cases, the tips of the fingers come into contact with each other, obstructing further rotation. In contrast, in a non-rotating scenario adorned with a co-axial counter-rotation, the theory does not hold true and observations show finger tips that overlap. The observed modes of finger structures in experiments are directly correlated with the balance of various forces, including membrane tension, centrifugal force, viscous forces, and the pressure difference across the membrane.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities of 1.9 x 10^9 cm^-2 and 2.8 x 10^8 cm^-2, respectively, as inferred from very weak spectral lines detected through the SubMillimeter Array. By comparing these observations with theoretical predictions for additional ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) isomers, the potential formation of the cyclopentadiene (C5H5CN) family was explored. Based on the cyclopentadiene (C5H5CN) family's formation rate being comparable to that of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) family, the possible presence of the cyclobutadiene (C4H4CCH) and cyclopropadiene (C3H3CCH) families was considered. Given the SubMillimeter Array's capability to detect these species, the case for further observation was made, as they could potentially be observable within a few hours, given the low expected formation of these complex molecules.

In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism enables the model to focus on specific parts of the source sentence when generating each target word. However, research reveals that words and positions following the currently generated target word carry more information and should ideally be considered with different importance. To address this limitation, we propose introducing a position-independent look-ahead attention mechanism that captures these varying importances and integrates them into a simple end-to-end attention model with minimal parameter changes. Our proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to the baseline standard attention across multiple datasets, showing that providing the generator with both forward and backward source information results in improved translation outcomes.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a similar disparity in complex software and challenging practical problems calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and deployment of grid computing. A translational perspective helps us understand why grid computing technology was developed the way it was, for better or worse. This perspective also clarifies how computing the world's weather involved both progress and limitations of grid computing. Comparing our analysis with existing interpretations of these topics reveals valuable insights. From this study, we derive several research opportunities within the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model that incorporates unified dark matter and energy aspects, with a choice of non-singular solutions based on a non-minimal scalar field with non-zero, negative, and time-dependent potential, is analyzed under a dissipative framework. By applying a non-zero, clockwise, and non-constant Hubble friction, the dynamics of an adiabatic universe are examined, with a focus on understanding the interplay between non-constant and time-varyer parameters. An iterative method is employed to derive the unified dark fluid's equation of state parameter and its associated non-constant adiabatic index, as well as the density profile, which can be expressed as $\rho \propto r^{-2\Gamma}$, where $\Gamma$ represents the non-constant adiabatic index derived through an integral of $\gamma(t)$. The resulting model exhibits well-behaved and dissipative characteristics with well-defined asymptotic behavior at large radii, with implications for adiabatic and polytropic indices, as well as gravitational collapse resistance. The model's dynamics can be further explored by considering the interplay between non-constant $\gamma(t)$ and a constant $\eta_0$, leading to a derived $\Gamma$ that influences the adiabatic index, pressure profile, and density profile, with $\rho \propto r^{-2\Gamma}$, where $\Gamma$ is a function of $\gamma(t)$ and $\eta_0$.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we analyzed J/ψ decay data from the BESIII experiment into both electron-neutrino and neutrinoless light sterile neutrino channels. By studying the decay processes, we determined limits on matrix elements and mediating forces, which help assess the viability of generic dark matter models. We found that without new interactions, the production of light sterile neutrino channels is highly restricted, with very long decay paths resulting in minimal missing energy. In contrast, dwarf galactic data suggests that certain mediating forces with specific parameters have limited dark matter parameter space for J/ψ invisible decay. Additionally, our research explored the implications for sub-GeV dark matter production through J/ψ invisible decay, with cross-section limits provided for neutrino dark matter interactions. By combining these findings with other experiments, we determined that J/ψ invisible decay excludes a large portion of the parameter space for type I light sterile neutrino scenarios, specifically with neutrinoless channels with mass values between 40 MeV and 60 MeV with a decay width greater than 10^-9 eV.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \in [0,+\infty)$ representing the walk's persistence and $\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))$ indicating a one-sided stable distribution. As the walk's persistence increases, the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ decreases, approaching 1 when $b=0$ and approaching $x$ as $b \to +\infty$.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and is supported by previous research and recent H-mode observations in the ICRF source.

While diagnosing cancer through microscopic image analysis is highly effective for experienced pathologists, it becomes unreliable and inconsistent when comparing different individuals. A key area where precise localization is crucial for accurate diagnosis is the identification of the nucleus in tissue images affected by cancer. Due to the nucleus being significantly smaller than the surrounding cytoplasm and lacking distinct texture, it presents a notably difficult target for detection algorithms. In this study, we develop a novel two-stage network, inspired by an existing architecture, to detect the nuclei within cancerous tissue images. This proposed model achieves superior performance in our experiments, demonstrating 31% higher accuracy, 25% higher recall, 30% higher F1 score, and 31% higher intersection over union compared to the baseline U-Net network.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNN baselines, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that identify distinctive graph attributes crucial for accurate predictions. Our hypothesis is supported by empirical evidence obtained through statistical analyses, controlled experiments, and direct visual inspections of synthesized and real data graphs. These results provide a practical guide for improving data-driven graph learning methods, including GCNN, by explicitly adjusting for the matched filtering approach. Our approach is demonstrated theoretically, computationally, and visually, setting a performance benchmark that surpasses current explanations of black-box deep learning models. Our code is available online at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/andrewswg/gcnn-filters.

In three-dimensional spacetime with a positive cosmological constant, a Chern-Simons action can be modified to include scalar and gauge fields. This altered action allows us to describe solitons and stable rotating configurations of these fields in the absence of black holes, as well as rotating black holes where the horizon sits at the edge of the bulk space. Using the phase space method, we can linearize small perturbations around these configurations and derive the corresponding gauge-coupled gravitoelectromagnetic spectrum, which features a shift in the harmonic frequencies due to the coupling strength and field configuration. This method can also be applied to the gravity-scalar field coupling from a Chern-Simons action, yielding a similar result. We further explore the non-linear spectrum via numerical solutions and confirm that our approach yields the same outcome.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualization and measurement of tissue mechanical properties, aiding the detection and differentiation of malignant tumors from benign lesions or healthy tissue. accurate measurement of shear waves, specifically their lateral displacement, is crucial in this process; however, achieving high-resolution elastography images in this area has been challenging due to limited acoustic data, particularly in deep tissue imaging scenarios with synthetic aperture reconstruction methods. Researchers developed a virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) reconstruction method to improve the resolution of acoustic images while maintaining contrast, leveraging the high-resolution envelope of virtual sources as point spread function (PSF) real sources. Although this method is computationally demanding, the team created an efficient algorithm to achieve full depth of field and symmetry in the VSSA PSF with just two adjustable parameters, streamlining the method to process thousands of frames per second on a single CPU. This breakthrough enables precise measurement of elastic shear waves' elastic images and opens up new possibilities for the clinical application of high-frequency ultrasound imaging.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This concept is an example of a broader relationship where the former can be considered as an applied version of the latter. This relationship gives rise to a new interpretation of the former, derived from the latter's dependence on the objects in the former. We propose an educational tool that demonstrates this connection, specifically designed for students studying computer science. This tool is called "Idea-based pseudocode," which bridges the gap between logical proofs and imperative algorithms by representing intermediate concepts such as arrays and linked lists. It uses concrete objects to make the abstract relationship more tangible and understandable.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the tendency of high-energy muons to remain at large angles and retain their energy as they undergo partonic radiation, the Effective Vector Boson Approximation (EVBAs) is not as applicable to them. Nonetheless, EVBAs serve as useful tools for estimating the production of both vector bosons and quarks at energy levels beyond reach, enabling the extraction of the partonic structure of quarks within a framework of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). This extraction of the "universal" PDFs of quarks is considered robust, and thus EVBAs should, in theory, be transferable across different quark types. In order to enhance the reliability of extraction of the partonic PDFs of quarks from experimental data of collider experiments, we have developed the Effective Parton Distribution of Weak Bosons in QCD (EPDWQ) code. This code accounts for the EPWs, which are distributions of PDFs of weak bosons and quarks, and can be utilized in the prediction of collider outcomes. It is designed to be code-agnostic and therefore applicable to a variety of code bases, including MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that using a
single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this challenge, we
investigate the benefits of using separate, modular learned models for each task.
Our experiments show that using a dedicated model for each task significantly
improves problem-solving performance in multi-task MRL with shared dynamics
models, especially when there are many tasks involved, allowing our approach
to scale effectively. Our method also performs well when combining modules
with different levels of optimization, showcasing the flexibility and
effectiveness of our approach.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, the Grela-Rosser Extension Theorem for Analytic Truth from 1953/1954, and Tarski's Theorem on the Undecidability of Semantic Consequences post-1949, demonstrating that Grela-Rosser's result is essentially a variation of Godel's incompleteness, which in turn is reducible to the undecidability of semantic truth.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers aim to recover the source of observed, often noisy, data. This recovery process yields not a singular solution but a set of probable solutions, known as the posterior distribution. While traditional methods focus on obtaining a single solution, our approach generates multiple samples from this distribution. The importance of such posterial sampling is due to its vast applications, including addressing decisions made under uncertainty. To effectively generate high-quality samples, we use GAN models to efficiently represent the posterior distribution. A regularized sample model then leverages GAN models to generate samples that adhere to various constraints inherent in inverse problems, effectively combining sample validity with distribution accuracy. Our method's efficiency is further enhanced by the use of auxiliary variables and gradient reversal layers, enabling model training with minimal computational cost. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through the resolution of tomographic and diffraction tomographic problems using real-world data, outperforming existing GAN-based methods in a broad range of tests, including those requiring Bayesian model comparison and model selection.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens that disrupt the signals emitted by distant radio pulsars, a critical tool for investigating the properties of these screens and the surrounding environment. In this study, we have reanalyzed the pulsar scintillation data collected by the Nancay Radio Telescope between 2013 and 2015, targeting the pulsar B1133+16 during multiple observation sessions, a period during which this pulsar passed through a specific line of sight near the galactic center. By combining different electron density maps, we identified a particular observation session where the pulsar traveled through a region of ionized gas known as HMXC-1, a hyper-velocity star remnant located 19.4 kpc from the Earth. By analyzing this specific interaction between the pulsar and HMXC-1, we have been able to closely scrutinize the properties of the local interstellar medium around HMXC-1, a rare opportunity to study these properties in our vicinity of the Milky Way, a feature not commonly found in most pulsars. This analysis has helped us to better understand the composition and structure of the ionized gas in this region of the galaxy.

This paper introduces a novel deep neural network architecture called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) for the generation of speech and singing voices. We enhanced the NoteNet model, which was previously introduced, by developing two major concepts: a quasi-periodic dilated network and a context-aware attention mechanism. The quasi-periodic dilated network adapts the network's filter bank in response to varying input pitches, thereby reducing the need for data augmentation and enhancing the model's transferability across different pitch ranges with fewer training samples. The context-aware attention mechanism, on the other hand, enables the model to capture long-range dependencies and structural information by dynamically adjusting filter banks based on the input context. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in the Mean Square Error metric and produces higher-fidelity waveforms in speech synthesis and polyphonic singing synthesis tasks.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames using spatial descriptions of visual content. Our approach does not rely on knowing specific scenarios or having access to extensive spatial language data. Instead, we circumvent the need for prior knowledge by using image-based representations, which efficiently capture the relationship between sounds and their corresponding visual sources. Our experiments show that our method can successfully locate sounds in both static and dynamic video environments, outperforming methods that use a combination of content and language information. Our findings also highlight the presence of distinctive, locally confined sound cues within video content.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but there is a significant need to develop robust representations in graphs embedded in hyperbolic space due to their inherent scalability and efficiency. We have observed that GCN representations suffer from limited translational invariance, which constrains their effectiveness. In response, we present a new method, LGCN, a novel network that combines LG-cocycles as features to capture local node relationships in a translation-invariant manner. Experimental results from node classification tasks on six datasets confirm the superior performance of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or harmonic counterparts.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this framework, temperature is inversely proportional to the entropy, specifically the change in system's microstates resulting from an energy increase. When a system's states become less likely with added energy, indicating an decrease in system's rigidity, negative temperature arises. This occurrence is associated with higher system's disorder and temperature, potentially approaching infinity, as seen in various physical systems, including certain spin systems, molecular vibrations, and even black hole radiation. Such negative temperatures are not impossible, but rather the most extreme manifestation of high energy states.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter space that meets all theoretical requirements, including those related to neutrino phenomena, WIMP dark matter behavior, and the stability of the vacuum. We also assess the implications for direct dark matter detection and directivity experiments, as well as for lepton flavor violation. Consequently, we identify the minimal set of new particles and interactions necessary to explain neutrino oscillations, the dark matter phenomenon, and the "atmospheric" and "solar" mass scales within the context of the Standard Model.

We employ exact diagonalization to investigate the influence of the $t_{2g}-e_g$ orbital mixing on various exact ground state properties within a Hubbard model specific to a square transverse cubane structure. By utilizing a unitary transformation, we convert the hydrogenic $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ symmetry structures into controllable parameters that influence the relevant wave functions. Our study reveals that the magnitude of $t_{2g}-e_g$ mixing has minimal impact on dimensionless properties as it lacks inherent meaning. However, when wave function properties such as the average distance between charged atoms are considered, the $t_{2g}-e_g$ mixing exerts a significant influence, particularly in molecules composed of early transition metal atoms located in the periodic table's lower middle section.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produced authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data, and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methods.
